b: Brazil's National Data Protection Agency (ANPD) has issued an English edition of its guidelines on who must comply with Law No. 15,211, the Digital Statute for Children and Adolescents known as the Digital ECA, and on what the law's general "duty of prevention" requires of those providers. The 69-page document is marked "Version 1.0" and "Digital publication (November 2026)", with no day given. The Portuguese original, which the ANPD states is the official version and prevails over the translation, was adopted on October 28, 2026, according to Digital Policy Alert and the Brazilian trade publication Mobile Time.

Brazil's data protection agency has published, in English, its official reading of who must follow the country's child online safety law and what the law's core prevention duty demands. It matters to any app, platform, game, AI chatbot or ad-funded service that children in Brazil can reach, including companies with no office in the country. Running age checks or other compliance tools does not take a service outside the law, and the agency, not the company, has the final word on whether a service is covered.

The guidelines set out to answer two questions, according to the introduction: "(i) to whom does the Digital ECA apply; and (ii) what are the meaning and implications of the duties of prevention, protection, information, and safety ('duty of prevention') for regulated entities." The document does not deal in detail with age assurance, parental supervision or content moderation. It says so plainly, while describing the duty of prevention as "the central foundation for the interpretation and application of these and other obligations provided for in the Digital ECA."

A 13-person drafting team wrote the text. Camila Leite Contri and Lucas Borges de Carvalho reviewed it, and the same two people oversaw the English translation, which, according to the document, "was generated using artificial intelligence." For direct citations of the statute, the ANPD used an English translation prepared by Brazil's Ministry of Human Rights and Citizenship, "with minor adaptations." The stated aim is "greater predictability and legal certainty in the application of the Law."

The law itself dates from September 17, 2025. It has been in force since March 17, 2026, and its implementing regulation, Decree No. 12,880, is dated March 18, 2026, according to the ANPD's English-language Digital ECA page. A draft of these guidelines went to public consultation on the Brasil Participativo platform from April 30 to June 15, 2026, according to a legal alert from the law firm Trench Rossi Watanabe and Digital Policy Alert's event record.
Location does not matter, and neither does price

The first finding is territorial. The Digital ECA applies "irrespective of its location, development, manufacture, provision, marketing, and operation" (Art. 1). The guidelines compare this with Article 11 of the Brazilian Civil Rights Framework for the Internet and Article 3 of the General Personal Data Protection Law (LGPD). A video game or a social media platform that is "available on the internet and likely to be accessed by children or adolescents in Brazil" falls under the law "even if, for example, the provider is a foreign company or is headquartered in another country."

The second finding concerns money. "The user's lack of direct payment, when analyzed in isolation, does not preclude the application of the Digital ECA's provisions," the ANPD writes. Users who do not pay in cash are often "part of a business model sustained by their data, advertising, or other indirect monetization mechanisms." The conclusion is explicit: "digital services based on advertising or other forms of indirect remuneration are subject to the Digital ECA, provided they are supplied remotely, electronically, and upon individual request."

The definition is also functional rather than tied to particular technologies. According to the guidelines, it can capture "marketplaces, messaging services, connected devices, and similar services" even though the law does not name them, and it is written to cover "both current and future technologies, even if they are not yet available to the public."
The three-part test for an information technology product or service

The statute defines an information technology product or service as one "provided remotely, by electronic means, and supplied in response to an individual request" (Art. 2, i). The guidelines break that into three elements, all of which must be present.
What the guidelines say it means
No simultaneous presence of the parties
Much of the trade in brick-and-mortar stores and shopping centres, even where electronic tools are used
Equipment and networks for transmission and processing, especially internet applications; hybrid devices such as augmented and virtual reality devices still count
Purely physical or offline services; services limited to telephone contact, such as telemarketing
Activation or use in response to a user's request, "without prejudice to the sharing of its use"
Broadcast transmissions aimed at an indeterminate audience

Shared use does not break the chain. Subscriptions to educational or streaming platforms used by several people in a household still involve an individual request, and "the Digital ECA remains applicable."

The law adjusts some obligations to the provider. Article 39 says the duties in Articles 6, 17, 18, 19, 20, 27, 28, 29, 31, 32 and 40 apply "according to the characteristics and functionalities of the information technology product or service, modulated according to the degree of interference of the provider of the product or service over the content made available, the number of users, and the size of the provider." Article 34, § 2 tells the ANPD to ensure "differentiated and proportionate treatment for services of different nature, risk, and business model."
Degree of interference over content made available

According to the guidelines, strictly educational, professional or public-interest platforms may receive different treatment. Other relevant aspects include whether a provider is for-profit or nonprofit, the type of content offered, the design standards adopted, "and the presence or absence of targeted advertising." The ANPD adds a warning in a boxed note: "Proportionality does not reduce the provider's responsibility; rather, it guides the form and scope of the expected measures." Every assessment must be done case by case.
The statute and the decree single out several types of provider for specific duties on top of the general ones. The guidelines take each in turn.
Link accounts of users up to 16 to a legal guardian (Art. 24); no behavioural profiles of minors for targeting commercial advertising (Art. 26)
Private messaging used for private communication; closed corporate, institutional or group applications
Verify age or age group (Art. 12, i); provide age information to app providers (Art. 12, iii); parental consent mechanism for downloads (Art. 12, § 2)
Marketplaces (Decree Art. 18); games and apps with in-app purchases
Provide an age signal to internet application providers
Obligations modulated for open-source systems used mainly by technical communities, and for closed environments such as Internet of Things appliances
Exempt from Art. 39 duties and from age assurance if safeguards apply (Art. 39, § 1; Decree Art. 22)
Platforms that host or recommend content submitted by end users
Provider of previously licensed copyrighted content
Same conditional exemptions as editorial-control services

The statute defines a social network as "an internet application whose primary purpose is the sharing and dissemination, by users, of opinions and information conveyed through text or image, audio, or audiovisual files on a single platform, via accounts that are connected or articulately accessible, allowing for connections between users." The guidelines read this through its effects: such services are "typically characterized by direct and widespread positive network externalities," meaning they become more valuable as more people join. "As a general rule," social media platforms are to be treated as directed at or likely to be accessed by children and adolescents.

Labels carry no weight. Classification "is based on the activity actually carried out by the provider, and not from its self-declaration or the trade name it uses." Article 19, § 2 of Decree No. 12,880/2026 makes the provider's own assessment non-binding on the ANPD, which "may, within the scope of its authority, determine a different classification at any time."

The document illustrates the line with a school example. A 15-year-old student uses a platform run by her school, available in app stores, with a login tied to her student number and a forum for real-time discussion. According to the ANPD, it is not a social network: sharing opinions is not the platform's primary purpose, the forum is "merely one of the platform's incidental features", and access is restricted to students and faculty.

App stores are defined as "an internet application that distributes and facilitates the download, for terminal users, of internet applications made available or accessible through its platform." Payment model does not matter: a store "may operate under free, paid, or hybrid models." The guidelines describe stores as "a first layer of agents with responsibilities" and add that they must provide "effective safeguards to prevent children and adolescents from entering into contractual or financial transactions without the proper supervision" of guardians.

Operating systems are "system software that controls the basic functions of hardware or software and allows internet applications, computer programs, apps, or other software to run through it." Because they come pre-installed and shape the device from first set-up, "a significant portion of the obligations under the Digital ECA falls on them," according to the ANPD. Together with app stores, they enable protection at scale, because "the same age assurance mechanism - in particular, the age signal - can be used by various apps accessed by children or adolescents."

Not every operating system is treated alike. Systems built on collaborative models and open source software, "which are primarily used in technical communities and have a low likelihood of being accessed by children and adolescents", are "not subject to the same obligations as proprietary operating systems used on a large scale by end users, especially children." The same modulation applies to systems on internet-connected home appliances. The guidelines also point to Article 2, § 2, which excludes from the definition "the functionalities essential to the operation of the Internet, such as the open and common technical protocols and standards."

A service with editorial control is "an internet application whose primary purpose is to make previously selected content available, without the use of automated selection methods, by a responsible economic agent." The exclusion of automated selection, the guidelines say, "presupposes some degree of human evaluation and curation." Video streaming, music streaming and digital libraries are the examples given. "The mere hosting or recommendation of content submitted by end users does not, in and of itself, fall under either of these scenarios."
These providers can skip age assurance under Article 22 of Decree No. 12,880/2026, provided that:

"i - they provide children's accounts or profiles with content appropriate for the age group of the child or adolescent, in accordance with the age rating system, when applicable; and ii - they implement parental supervision, blocking systems, or restrictions on children's and adolescents' access to content, while respecting progressive autonomy and age ratings, where applicable."

Journalistic and sports content not subject to ratings and under editorial control is exempt from age assurance outright. They are also exempt from the Article 29 duty to remove content that violates children's rights upon notification, which the guidelines say applies "particularly" to services "such as social media platforms" where users share content "without any prior human curation or licensing." The exemption has a ceiling, though: it "does not exempt the provider from the duty to adopt the most protective settings by default (Article 7 of the Digital ECA) or from the other obligations under the Digital ECA."
"Likely access" and the eight presumed categories

The phrase that stretches the law beyond services built for children is "likely access". Under the sole paragraph of Article 1, a product or service is considered likely to be accessed by children and adolescents when three conditions are met:

"i - sufficient likelihood of use and attractiveness of the information technology product or service by children and adolescents; ii - considerable ease of access to and use of the information technology product or service by children and adolescents; and iii - a significant degree of risk to the privacy, safety, or biopsychosocial development of children and adolescents, especially in the case of products or services intended to enable social interaction and large-scale information sharing among users in a digital environment."

All three must be present. A service that is attractive and easy to reach but carries no significant risk is not "likely to be accessed". The ANPD immediately closes the door on narrow readings: interpretations that undermine protections "must not be accepted," and the test must follow the principle of the best interests of the child.
For eight categories, no test is needed. The Digital ECA and Decree No. 12,880/2026 create a legal presumption of likely access for:
"systems capable of generating content and interacting with users based on natural language instructions", listed in the appendix as generative artificial intelligence systems;
e-commerce platforms "that facilitate the purchase and sale of products and services prohibited for children and adolescents."
The presumption "may only be rebutted with proper justification," and only where one or more of the three Article 1 requirements is shown not to be met in the specific case.
Compliance does not create an exit

Can a provider that verifies ages then argue that children no longer reach it? According to the guidelines, no. Measures adopted to comply with the law, such as age assurance mechanisms, "cannot be considered sufficient to rule out any of the requirements set forth in the sole paragraph of Article 1 of the Law." The document lays out the order of operations: first determine whether the law applies, then comply. Age assurance "constitutes compliance with a legal obligation that follows the determination of the Law's applicability, rather than a factor that precludes likely access."

The ANPD spells out why: "A different interpretation would lead to a circular argument: compliance with a legal obligation would remove the provider from the scope of the regulation that imposes it, which would authorize the elimination of the measure itself and, consequently, reestablish the conditions for likely access." The same logic applies to risk mitigation in general. Age assurance "does not preclude the application of the 'likely access' criterion (and the Law itself) to the provider, even if it is considered that the implemented measures have mitigated the risks involved."

A stated target audience does not settle the matter either. "What matters is the combination of the product's characteristics and actual conditions of use, not merely the provider's indication of who its intended recipients are."
Attractiveness, ease of access, and risk

On attractiveness, the guidelines list factors such as "language, visual aesthetics, themes, characters, rewards, gamification, the use of influencers, engagement dynamics," even when nothing is explicitly aimed at children. Elements that look neutral alone may matter "when combined with notifications, rewards, rankings, and personalization."

On ease of access, the document points to simplified onboarding, low technical requirements and compatibility with common devices. It cites the TIC Kids Online Brazil 2025 survey from the Brazilian Network Information Center: 96% of internet users aged 9 to 17 went online through a mobile phone in 2025, and daily phone use reached 90% of users, rising to 98% among those aged 15 to 17. Accessibility features built for people with disabilities, older people or users with low digital literacy are not, "in isolation," evidence of ease of access.

A second worked example concerns a 10-year-old who wants to join a social media platform of short videos on professional make-up, popular with her classmates, that lets anyone "Sign in with an email account" already on the device. The provider says the product targets professionals, not children. According to the ANPD's analysis, the "simplified user registration processes result in considerable ease of access," so the second requirement is met.

On risk, the guidelines define it as the possibility of negative effects on privacy, safety or biopsychosocial development, "taking into account the probability of occurrence and the potential severity of the consequences." Services that enable large-scale social interaction and information sharing carry a presumption of significant risk. The assessment covers the operation as a whole, including "business model, features, architecture, recommendation and interaction mechanisms, personal data processing flows, usage patterns, engagement strategies, methods of content delivery." A third example describes a 14-year-old on a social media platform for messages, short videos and audio clips, whose recommender systems drew on message history, interaction patterns and usage time without explaining how it worked. The ANPD finds significant risk across all three dimensions, including "unsupervised contact with adults."

The evidence that points towards likely access, according to the guidelines, includes "the display of advertising targeted at children and adolescents", content and design attractive to minors, similarity to presumed categories, and "actual access or use by children and adolescents, based on available evidence, including data from the platform itself or from independent research and studies." A boxed note says this evidence is "solely for illustrative and auxiliary purposes" and adds no legal requirement.
How the likely access test works
According to Appendix iii of the guidelines, the flowchart for deciding whether the Digital ECA applies has six steps:
Determine whether the provider offers an information technology product or service. If not, "The Digital ECA does not apply."
Determine whether the provider explicitly states that the product or service is intended for children and adolescents, for example in its terms of use or description. If so, the law applies.

If not, determine whether the provider falls into one of the eight categories with a legal presumption of likely access under the Digital ECA and Decree No. 12,880/2026. If so, "Likely access is presumed unless proven otherwise."
Otherwise, conduct the likely access test, in which the three requirements of Article 1, sole paragraph, must be met cumulatively.

Apply the test "Always in accordance with the best interests principle," using supporting evidence such as content of interest to minors, attractive design, advertising targeted at minors, similarity to presumed services, and actual use.
If all three requirements are met, the product or service is likely to be accessed by children and adolescents. If not, likely access is not characterized.

A closing note on the appendix repeats that "The provider's self-assessment is not binding" and that the ANPD may reach a different conclusion, including on the differentiated treatment under Articles 34 and 39.
The duty of prevention in four parts

Article 5 requires covered providers to observe "the duties of prevention, protection, information, and safety provided for in this Chapter and in Law No. 8,078, of September 11, 1990 (Consumer Defense Code), and in Law No. 8,069, of July 13, 1990 (Child and Adolescent Statute)." The guidelines group these under one umbrella, the duty of prevention in the broad sense, and define it as "the legal obligation of providers of information technology products or services to act proactively and diligently by adopting appropriate, proportionate, and effective measures that, throughout the life cycle of the products and services, prevent or mitigate risks of violations of children's and adolescents' rights and protect their best interests."
"the duty to prevent risks to the privacy, safety, and health of children and adolescents in the digital environment"
"the duty to ensure the comprehensive, special, and priority protection of children's and adolescents' rights in the digital environment, guided by their best interests"
Clear, accessible information about products and services, prospectively and through semiannual transparency reports

"the duty to prevent the occurrence of accidental or unlawful situations that result in the improper processing of children's and adolescents' personal data, or that impact their life, health, and physical and psychological well-being"

The dimensions overlap. Default settings at the most protective level, for instance, satisfy both protection and safety. The model "shifts from reacting to harm to preventing it," and providers must "demonstrate the measures they have adopted to comply with the law." Effectiveness "must be supported by evidence documented by the regulated entities."

Article 6 requires reasonable measures "from the design stage and throughout the operation" against six categories of content, products or practices. Two of them concern advertising directly: "iv - promotion and commercialization of games of chance, fixed-odds betting, lotteries, tobacco products, alcoholic beverages, narcotics, or products whose sale is prohibited to children and adolescents" and "v - predatory, unfair, or deceptive advertising practices, or other practices known to cause financial harm to children and adolescents." The others are sexual exploitation and abuse; physical violence, cyberbullying and harassment; inducement to self-harm, suicide, substance use, self-diagnosis or self-medication; and pornographic content.

Article 7 requires providers to "ensure, by default, the most protective settings available regarding privacy and personal data protection," and § 1 says the service "shall, by default, operate with the highest level of privacy and personal data protection." Article 8 adds five duties, among them to "develop, from the design stage, and adopt by default settings that prevent the compulsive use of products or services by children and adolescents."
According to the guidelines, the duty to manage risks under Article 8, i and Article 47 of the decree follows four steps:

Identify risks at three levels: functionalities, such as private instant messaging; resources, such as hardware, integrated AI models and end-to-end encryption; and systems, "from the user interface to the operating system."
Assess likelihood and severity under Decree Art. 47. The ANPD recommends indicating a risk level, "low, medium, or high", based on clear criteria.
Adopt measures and safeguards to prevent and mitigate the risks.

Document and demonstrate effectiveness, including "tests and data used to assess whether the measures are achieving the expected results" and "metrics that allow for monitoring, over time, the effectiveness."

The guidelines point to outside references for classifying risks. They cite the European Commission's guidelines on protecting minors under Article 28(4) of the Digital Services Act, published in the Official Journal on October 10, 2025, the OECD's "5Cs" typology (content, conduct, contact, consumer and cross-cutting risks), the "4Cs" model (content, contact, conduct and contract), and the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights. A fourth example shows the expected standard in practice: a platform's internally tested classifier flags coordinated insults on a 15-year-old's post, human moderators confirm harassment, the content is removed, the accounts are suspended, and the teenager is told why and offered an appeal.

The duty of protection is where advertising rules sit. The guidelines cite "the prohibition on the use of profiling techniques to target commercial advertising at children and adolescents, as well as the use of emotional analysis, augmented reality, extended reality, and virtual reality for this purpose (Art. 22)," plus the prohibition on abusive advertising and the marketing restrictions on betting, lotteries, tobacco, alcohol and narcotics in Articles 31 and 32 of Decree No. 12,880/2026.

The duty to inform "should not be confused with merely formal transparency, nor is it satisfied by simply making available lengthy, technical, or difficult-to-understand texts." The guidelines list three ways to meet it: age-appropriate language with visual aids, prominent display of the most relevant information, and communication "at appropriate points in the user flow without disrupting the regular user experience." Designs that "conceal risks, obscure essential information, make it difficult to reverse choices, or induce decisions contrary to the best interests of children and adolescents" are incompatible with the duty. Article 18, § 2 prohibits providers "to design, modify, or manipulate interfaces with the purpose or effect of compromising the user's autonomy, decision-making, or choice", the conduct usually called a dark pattern.

Semiannual transparency reports under Article 31 are the main retrospective instrument. They apply "only to providers with more than 1,000,000 (one million) registered users in the age group of children and adolescents who have an internet connection within the national territory." According to the guidelines, the reports must cover complaint channels and investigation processes, the number of complaints, the volume of content or account moderation by type, measures to identify unlawful acts and children's accounts on social media, technical improvements for data protection and parental consent verification, and the methods and results of impact assessments. Editorial-control and licensed-content providers are exempt if they meet the conditions in Article 39, § 1, items i to iv.

The fifth example will interest marketers. A 13-year-old signs up for a dance game, "DançaTech", which streams his movements and images of his living room to other users after he accepts standard terms. Days later, his guardians find clips of his dancing in the game's promotional materials. The ANPD calls this a violation of the duty to inform and adds that "the use of images of children and adolescents for commercial promotional purposes requires authorization from their legal guardians, which was also not obtained in this case."

Finally, the duty of safety scales with reach. "The greater the capacity to amplify, direct, or facilitate interactions and content accessible to children and adolescents, and the greater the platform's reach, the greater the burden of demonstrating that security is built into the design and continuously maintained during operation."
Why this matters for advertisers and platforms

The guidelines turn several of the statute's open phrases into working definitions, and most of them widen rather than narrow the law. Ad-funded services are expressly covered. The presence of targeted advertising is a factor in how obligations are modulated, and advertising aimed at children is listed as evidence of likely access. Generative AI chat services and e-commerce sites selling products barred to minors are presumed to be in scope, alongside the app stores and operating systems that sit underneath them.

The ANPD has spent the past year building towards this. PPC Land reported in December 2025 that the agency added child protection to its 2026-2027 enforcement agenda, with 15 inspections planned on privacy-by-default for child-directed services and five actions on secondary use of data for targeted advertising. In May 2026, the agency released a preliminary age verification guide for public input that rejected self-declaration as a reliable method and said verification data may not be used for behavioural advertising or profiling.

Enforcement has followed. On August 12, 2026, the ANPD ordered Discord to suspend its Go Live feature for Brazilian users within three business days, in a case where fines under Article 35 of the Digital ECA can reach R$50 million per infraction. Weeks later, an ANPD investigation report recommended fines of R$153.7 million against ByteDance over TikTok's handling of children's data under the LGPD. App store operators have moved too. Apple began requiring a Brazilian betting licence for gambling apps on its App Store in May 2026, and its July 2026 social media questions for app age ratings map to an A16 rating in Brazil.

Brazil is not working alone. The guidelines draw on the European Commission's Digital Services Act guidance on minors, and in September 2026 the Commission went further with a proposal to bar under-15s from autonomous social media accounts. Brazil's government had already used other tools before the Digital ECA took effect, including an extrajudicial notice to Meta over AI chatbots simulating child profiles in August 2025.

For companies outside Brazil, the territorial finding is probably the most consequential. A product built elsewhere, priced at zero and funded by advertising, with no Brazilian office, is still a "provider of information technology products or services" if children in Brazil can reach it and the three likely access conditions hold. Its own view of its audience counts for little.

The document sets no numeric thresholds for "number of users" or "size of the provider" under Article 39, apart from the one-million-user trigger for transparency reports, and it does not say what evidence would be enough to rebut the presumption for the eight categories. Age assurance methods, parental supervision and content moderation are left to other instruments. The appendix summarising likely access emphasises the 4Cs model, while the body text cites both the 4Cs and the OECD's 5Cs. The English edition gives no day of publication.

Who: Brazil's National Data Protection Agency (ANPD), which enforces the Digital ECA, and every provider of information technology products or services directed at or likely to be accessed by children and adolescents in Brazil, including social networks, app stores, operating systems, games, generative AI systems and ad-funded services based abroad.

What: A 69-page guidance document, now available in English, that defines who the Digital ECA covers, sets out a three-part "likely access" test with a legal presumption for eight categories of provider, rules out age checks and other compliance measures as a way out of scope, and breaks the duty of prevention into prevention, protection, information and safety.
When: The Portuguese original was adopted on October 28, 2026; the English edition is marked Version 1.0, November 2026. The law has been in force since March 17, 2026.
Where: Brazil, with effect for any provider worldwide whose products or services children in Brazil can access, regardless of where the provider is located.

Why: The ANPD says the guidelines aim to bring "greater predictability and legal certainty" to a law built on prevention, so that providers know whether they are covered and what they must be able to demonstrate before the agency acts.
